description:
Hermes Group es un equipo multidisciplinario especializado en desarrollo de software, ingeniería de sistemas, ciberseguridad y análisis de datos. Combinamos infraestructura propia, procesamiento de información y tecnologías de visualización avanzada para transformar datos complejos en soluciones funcionales. Nos mueve la exploración científica, la investigación aplicada y el desarrollo de herramientas que permitan comprender nuestro planeta y el espacio desde nuevas perspectivas.

Hermes Group is a multidisciplinary team specializing in software development, systems engineering, cybersecurity, and data analysis. We combine self-hosted infrastructure, information processing, and advanced visualization technologies to transform complex data into practical solutions. We are driven by scientific exploration, applied research, and the development of tools that enable us to better understand our planet and space from new perspectives.
summary: Satellites have watched fire in South America for 25 years, but the record is split in two. MODIS has seen the ground in 1 km pixels since 2000, and VIIRS in 375 m pixels since 2012. If you count detections, 2012 looks like the year fire exploded. It did not: the sensor changed. Theyt puts both sensors on one fair scale. Tested on years it never saw, its annual error is 4%, against 71% for a raw count. It then turns that record into a burning calendar for any place in Chile and Argentina, from 2001 to today, and it shows whether this month runs above normal. On top of that record runs the **Theyt engine, our own processing of 4.6 million detections plus live GOES-19 and CONAF data. It tells real wildfires from volcanoes and industry (AUC 0.99 on years it never saw), forecasts danger for the week ahead, and sends firefighters alerts. The calendar for any area is calculated from our own harmonized archive in seconds, without waiting on external services. Spread is calculated by our own pipeline: Cell2Fire-W, fed with our fuel map from satellite land cover, real slope and hourly weather, with our own McArthur-based model as a backup. That pipeline estimates where a fire could be in 1, 3 and 6 hours and gives the fastest route there. Our own map agent answers questions in plain words in a few seconds. It reads only Theyt engine data and shows what it used. A memory of past fires, told through satellite images and the people who lived them, completes the app.
details:
VIIRS true color, 3 February 2024: smoke from the Viña del Mar fire blowing over the Pacific. NASA GIBS.

The problem

On 3 February 2024, NASA satellites recorded 440 fire detections in a single day over Viña del Mar, Chile. Every fire season, people in Chile and Argentina ask the same questions. Is this year worse than normal? When does my area burn? Where is this fire going, and how do we get there?

The data to answer the first two questions has existed for 25 years in NASA FIRMS, but nobody can compare across it fairly. MODIS (2000 onward, 1 km) and VIIRS (2012 onward, 375 m) count fire differently. VIIRS sees the same fire with many more pixels and catches smaller fires. Before mid-2002 only Terra was flying, so there were fewer passes per day. A raw count therefore shows false jumps that have nothing to do with fire.

The Theyt engine: from raw satellite data to answers for firefighters

Theyt does not just put FIRMS on a map. It runs its own engine, which takes raw data from more than 15 sources and turns it into answers people can act on.

What it processes

  • 5.2 million MODIS and VIIRS detections over Chile and Argentina (2000 to 2025). After cleaning, 4.6 million remain, grouped into fire cell-days on one H3 grid. The full archive runs in about one minute.
  • Near real time data, refreshed every 3 hours from FIRMS (MODIS, VIIRS Suomi NPP and NOAA-20), every 10 minutes from GOES-19, and every 5 minutes from CONAF's official fires.
  • Weather, terrain and fuel for every cell: ERA5-Land and Open-Meteo, 30 m slope, and 10 m land cover translated to CONAF's KITRAL fuel types.

What it computes, one layer on top of the other

The orange line is the raw count, which jumps when VIIRS starts. The blue line is Theyt's harmonized series.

  • Common unit: a fire cell-day. Each detection falls into a hexagonal H3 cell of about 5 km², and each cell counts once per day, however many pixels marked it. This removes most of the pixel-size effect.
  • Calibration: MODIS is calibrated against VIIRS over the 14 years both satellites flew (2012 to 2025), for each month and zone. The global factor is 2.04 and stays stable year to year (1.81 to 2.17). A second correction (2.67) covers the Terra-only years before Aqua.
  • Cleaning: only vegetation fires are kept. Detections that the archive marks as volcanoes, industry or other static sources are removed.
  • Validation: each year from 2012 to 2025 was held out in turn. The median annual error is 4% for the harmonized series against 71% for a raw count. By zone and month, r = 0.96. Against CONAF's official burned area, Spearman = 0.71 for the 2002 to 2024 seasons.
  • Second version: a gradient boosting model trained on 4.6 million detections. It replaced nothing until it beat the first method at every scale on years it never saw. The place-by-place median error went from 46% to 37%. Both versions are published side by side at theyt.app/data.

2. A burning calendar for any place.

Calendar for Greater Valparaíso: every month since 2001 on the harmonized scale, the current month against its median, and the fires CONAF reported in the municipality.

To get a calendar, you draw an area, pick a saved one or type coordinates. Theyt shows which months burn and which years were worst. It also shows the current month's pace against its historical median. Next to the satellite record are the fires CONAF reported in that municipality. A toggle switches between raw and harmonized counts so the difference is visible. Monthly counts and hot spots download as CSV.

3. Following a fire in progress.

An official CONAF fire, with MODIS/VIIRS detections within 5 km in the last 48 hours, GOES-19 scans and the trend.

When you tap a hot spot, Theyt gathers everything around it: MODIS and VIIRS, GOES-19 every 10 minutes, and the official CONAF incident. It tells you whether the fire is growing or easing. It also warns when a hot spot is a volcano, a mine or a smelter rather than a forest. Our own classifier, trained on 25 years of each place's history, makes that call.

4. Spread, danger and response.

Estimated spread at 1, 3 and 6 hours with Cell2Fire-W (Universidad de Chile), KITRAL fuel types from satellite land cover, real slope and the hourly forecast.

  • Spread: where a fire could be in 1, 3 and 6 hours, with a range rather than a single line.
  • 7-day danger: a forecast of fire danger for the week ahead, compared with what is normal for that date. AUC is 0.81, against 0.76 for seasonality alone.
  • Response, for signed-in fire teams: the fastest route from the nearest station with live traffic, plus nearby hydrants.

Theyt is a support tool. It does not replace official dispatch.

5. Reports and memory.

Memory: major fires across Latin America, each one with satellite images from before, during and after the fire, its hot spots and photos with author and license.

Penco, Chile, 17 January 2026. Photo by a member of our team. That night, satellites recorded 1,072 fire detections there.

People can report smoke or fire from the map. Reports are stored on our server, never published automatically, and shown with the satellite data around them. The Memory section tells major fires in Chile, Argentina and the rest of Latin America, using what the satellites saw and the people who lived them. The team's own cases come first.

6. Ask the map.

Questions in plain words, answered only with Theyt data, with a list of the data it used.

The map agent is our own. It runs an open model, and the only tools it has are calls to the Theyt engine: the harmonized calendar of an area, this month against its median, fires in progress near a point, CONAF reports by municipality and the 7-day danger. Someone without time to read charts gets the answer straight away, for example "Is anything burning near Quilpué?" or "Is this February worse than normal here?". It never makes up numbers: when a tool does not return a value, the agent says so.

Who it helps

  • Firefighters get alerts already filtered of volcanoes and industry, and they see where a fire is, where it is going and how to reach it, with the nearby hydrants.
  • Families see their fire season and whether this month is above normal, and can report smoke.
  • Planners and researchers get 25 years of comparable data for any area, with downloads and an open API.

How we built it

Theyt is an open web app with a 3D globe (CesiumJS, React, TypeScript, ECharts) and a Node server. The data pipeline is in Python (DuckDB, Polars, H3, scikit-learn, statsmodels, Google Earth Engine). The app runs on an Oracle Cloud ARM server behind a Cloudflare tunnel. Automated tests cover the app in a real browser (Playwright), the code (Vitest, pytest) and the science, using leave-one-year-out validation. Every validation number on this page comes from a script that anyone can run again.

What is new

FIRMS and Global Forest Watch show each sensor separately, and GWIS gives fire seasonality only at country scale. Theyt harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS into one series with a published error, brings it down to any polygon or municipality, and checks it against official records. It then connects where fire has burned historically with how long help takes to get there.

Honest limits

  • The Cell2Fire validation against the Viña del Mar 2024 fire got the burned area in the right order of magnitude but the wrong spread direction. The hit rate was about 0.3, and we show this openly.
  • Fire station and hydrant data in Chile is shown only to signed-in teams and is never redistributed.

Next

Chile and Argentina today, the rest of Latin America next, then anywhere with fire.
